newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing saga enters new stage.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing saga enters new stage.

text.p: Lawyers for Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh began staking out ground on Monday to appeal his conviction and death sentence as the state of Oklahoma said it would try him for mass murder this year.

Michael Tigar, lawyer for alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols, meanwhile, asked federal trial judge Richard Matsch not to disclose how much taxpayer money was spent defending McVeigh, a figure published reports have put as high as $10 million. Nichols is to go on trial sometime this year.
Tigar said in a court filing on Friday he was concerned that revealing how the money was spent would make public the investigative leads that McVeigh's attorneys followed.

"Allowing the public and therefore the government to learn those avenues of defence that the McVeigh team investigated ... would give the prosecution unfair insight into potential Nichols defence strategies," he wrote.
A jury on Friday sentenced McVeigh to die by lethal injection for the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal office building that killed 168 people and injured more than 500 others.

McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones, who has come under criticism from some lawyers for his strategy in admitting his client's guilt in the penalty phase of the case, said on Monday he was planning appeals. Legal experts said the appeals could take years to work their way through the legal system.

Jones told CBS television's "This Morning" programme that possible issues for appeal include Matsch's refusal to grant the defence a delay in the trial after the Dallas Morning News published a report alleging McVeigh had confessed to his attorneys -- a charge Jones has denied.

Two other issues that could figure in an appeal are Matsch's refusal to let the defence present witnesses who would testify about a possible international conspiracy that Jones says may lie behind the bombing, and the judge's refusal to admit a Justice Department report highly critical of work done by the Federal Bureau of Investigation crime laboratory.
As McVeigh's lawyers staked out grounds for appeal, Oklahoma vowed to push ahead with plans to try McVeigh in the state for the bombing.

Oklahoma City District Attorney Robert Macy said, also on CBS television, the state planned to try McVeigh there for the deaths of 160 people in the bombing. In his federal trial McVeigh was convicted only of murdering eight federal agents who were working in the federal building.

Asked why another trial was needed when McVeigh was already sentenced to die, Macy said: "There's always a possibility it could be overturned on appeal. The statute under which they prosecuted is a special statute and it has not been reviewed by the U.S. Supreme Court."
He said 26 percent of all death penalties handed down in the past 20 years have been overturned on appeal.

He said he had promised the people of Oklahoma City he would try the alleged bombers in Oklahoma "and I feel I have to honour that promise." But a state trial for McVeigh would not be held until after Nichols' federal trial and it probably would be as late as November before state charges are filed.
Several defence lawyers have criticised the McVeigh defence team's decision to admit in the penalty phase of the trial that the 29-year-old ex-soldier was guilty.

Denver death penalty specialist David Lane told USA Today, "I don't know what the hell they were doing. ... First they said their man is innocent, then they come back with this. The jury had to be saying, 'You guys were lying to us.'"

Jones told the CBS programme "60 minutes" on Sunday that there was evidence to suggest that McVeigh "may simply have been a patsy, that he may have been used and involved by others as ... sort of a convenient fall guy."
Jones said he knew that other people with connections in Germany and the Middle East had an interest in blowing up the Murrah federal building several years ago.
